newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Show celebrates birth of Italian consumer society.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Show celebrates birth of Italian consumer society.

text.p: - Italians are flocking to glimpse a vanished fantasy world where cars become airborne, a soot-covered chick rails against the injustices of the world and a cowboy riding a cigar-chomping horse sets the world to rights.

An exhibition dedicated to a celebrated TV advertising show, broadcast daily from the mid-1950s for two decades, has mined a rich vein of nostalgia among Italians, recalling a time when life seemed simpler than in the world-weary 1990s.

The show captures an air of boundless optimism in stark contrast with the mood of brooding self-doubt afflicting Italy today as the country grapples with high unemployment, rising crime and a drawn-out institutional crisis.

The fable-like quality of many of the advertising shorts and a sense of almost childish wonder at the arrival of cheap cars, washing machines and creature comforts is also at odds with the brash, no-holds-barred commercialism of present-day Italy.
NOSTALGIA FOR BOOM YEARS

The show, called Carosello, was grafted in the memory of generations of Italians who grew up in the 1950s and 60s and, as children, were ritually packed off to bed by their parents as soon as the programme was over.
"As a child, when the programme went on the air, you never wanted it to end because you knew you would get sent to bed afterwards," said Anna Masera, a journalist with weekly magazine Panorama.

The show, always broadcast after the main evening news bulletin, stood out as the highlight of the day's entertainment at a time when state television RAI provided leaden fare on the country's only channel.
Carosello shows, introduced by a distinctive signature tune accompanying a scene of a theatre curtain being raised, featured four or five film-tableaux or cartoons.

The sketches are a colourful chronicle of the way Italians were in the boom years of the 1950s and 60s but also provide telling images of the making of a vibrant consumer society in a country rapidly hauling its way out of poverty.
"These films make one smile. It's like looking at photos taken of oneself 20 years ago," said Laura Minestroni, a writer and broadcaster on advertising.
A DIFFERENT KIND OF ADVERT
Carosello was the only outlet for television advertising until rival commercial TV stations were established in the 1970s.
The films were self-contained and usually had nothing to do with the product they were promoting under strict rules laid down by SIPRA, a state company that regulated TV advertising.
A short endorsement by a screen personality rounded off each 135-second episode.
Some of the big talents of Italian theatre and cinema, including playwright Dario Fo and film director Ettore Scola, cut their teeth making shorts for Carosello.

A celebrated advert, scripted by Fo, who later won international acclaim for his play "Accidental death of an Anarchist", tells the tale of how a bumbling private detective called Joe La Volpe overcomes all odds to catch outlaws.

The secret to his success is a new brand of petrol (gasoline) launched in 1956 by state oil company Agip, called Supercortemaggiore, which gives his car a surge of power allowing him to overhaul runaway criminals.
But in a film starring singer Domenico Modugno, rival petrol company API promised that its own brand could go one better.

Modugno, driving an Alfa Romeo sportscar, fills his tank up with API and as he bursts into song with Volare (Flying), the tune that made him world famous, his car soars above the traffic and becomes airborne.
ADVERTISING ICONS
Blown-up models of Carosello icons are displayed at the exhibition.

Favourites include a blue hippopotamus called Pippo, used to advertise a brand of baby nappies, and Coco Bill, a gun-slinging cowboy on a horse smoking a cigar who endorsed an ice cream brand called Eldorado.
But the star of the show, at the Triennale Hall in central Milan, is a sooty-faced chick covered in eggshell with a doleful expression called Calimero, popular until the 1970s.

In a tale with racist overtones, a tearful Calimero is shunned because he is black. He laments the injustice of his plight until a maiden tells him "you are not black, just dirty" and plunges him into a basin with soapy water.
Calimero emerges white and singing the praises of the washing powder used to scrub him clean.
Carosello eventually fell victim to the commercialism that it helped engender.

"Carosello was an elitist instrument because only a few select companies were able to advertise on it," said Antonio Pilati, a Milan-based commentator on media affairs. "When state television lost its monopoly, Carosello went with it."
